top.line: Ship, get profitable, raise from strength, and open everything
top.para: A startup operating and investing model in three pillars. Ship something usable, give it away briefly, then take it away to see if anyone notices; be profitable before raising, so investors call you; and open source everything, because technology was never the moat. Each pillar buys the position needed for the next.

s0.line: Shipping means a usable product, not a demo
s0.para: A startup makes something people buy at a price profitable to you, so the key skill is shipping daily: a thing a stranger can use alone, however rough. Keep running costs near nothing with serverless and minimal state; here the file system is the database. Getting the product into strangers' hands is the first real product.

s1.line: Give it away briefly, then check they miss it
s1.para: Offer the product free for a short window, which surfaces dozens of access and usability problems. Then deliberately take it away, without changing anything or apologising, and ask whether people miss it. A shrug means people only accept it while free, with no why now to sell; people coming back asking for it means you have something.

s2.line: Price must satisfy buyers and still be profitable
s2.para: Ask both whether buyers happily pay the price and whether it is profitable, allowing for a gap that scale will close if you can self fund it. Revenue comes first and profitability changes everything. Avoid default subscriptions: subscriptions.sgit.ai argues they are a discount for regular use, and pay on demand is usually healthier.

s3.line: Raise only after profitability, from a position of strength
s3.para: The worst time to raise is before profit, product or fit, when you bargain from weakness against a clock. Profit buys time, and the worst terms hand control to investors whose focus is misaligned, a common self-inflicted failure. As in music, do not sign before you have the album; raise from strength, on your terms.

s4.line: Open sourcing everything strengthens rather than gives away value
s4.para: Five reasons: technology is not the moat, so openness forces you to find what is defensible; code for strangers has cleaner architecture; open source normalises throwing things away; customers can read rather than trust; and founders keep their tools when they leave. Open source is a strategy, not a charity. A 2 October 2026 follow-up continues it.

s5.line: Encrypted vaults make cheap, reversible shipping possible
s5.para: Every pillar needs shipping to be cheap, fast and reversible, which vaults provide: data, app, history and sources travel as one string with no database, hosting, account or install. The published estate is 2,662 files and 295 MB, opened with one read key. That loop, open source throughout, is what Dinis wants others to have.
